# Platform limits

<!-- Generated by scripts/generate-platform-limits.ts from the adapter capability maps and the console catalog. Do not edit by hand. -->

Agentship automates everything the App Store Connect and Google Play APIs expose, and hands
back structured instructions for everything else. This page is the honest boundary between
the two, generated from the code that enforces it.

Read the columns as:

- **API** — Agentship does it for you.
- **API (you approve)** — Agentship does it, after you approve that exact change. Money,
  privacy, review submissions and anything reaching production always land here.
- **API (needs a value)** — Agentship needs something from you before it can act.
- **Console** — no API exists. Agentship gives your agent the exact page, steps and values;
  an agent with a browser may follow them after showing you what it will submit.
- **Console (you)** — no API exists *and* you must do it yourself: identity, money,
  agreements, two-factor. Never let an agent attempt these.
- **—** — the store has no such concept, or Agentship deliberately does not touch it.

## Work with no API

Every entry below is real console work, with the page it lives on and the date the
instructions were last checked against that page. Agentship proposes the values it already
knows and verifies the result afterwards where the store lets it be verified.

### App Store Connect

#### Agreements, tax and banking

| Operation | Id | Who does it | Why it cannot be an API call | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Accept agreements and complete tax and banking details | `apple:agreements-tax-banking` | You, personally | Apple requires the Account Holder to accept the Paid Applications agreement and to supply tax and banking information in person. None of it is exposed by the App Store Connect API. These are legal acceptances and financial identity details tied to one named person. An agent must never accept an agreement on someone's behalf, and must never see or type a bank account, a tax identifier or an identity document. | 2026-08-03 |

#### Credentials

| Operation | Id | Who does it | Why it cannot be an API call | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Create the App Store Connect API key | `apple:api-key` | You, personally | API keys are issued in App Store Connect by a user with the Admin or Account Holder role. There is no API that creates an API key — that would be a bootstrap Apple does not offer. Creating the key requires a signed-in App Store Connect session with two-factor authentication, and the download hands over a private key. Agentship stores that key through agentship_configure_auth and never sees the console session. | 2026-08-03 |

#### Privacy declarations

| Operation | Id | Who does it | Why it cannot be an API call | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Declare App Privacy data use | `apple:app-privacy` | You or your agent | App Privacy answers are not in the public App Store Connect API — verified against the 4.4.1 OpenAPI specification, which has no data-use resource — and they are a legal declaration about what the app really does. | 2026-08-03 |

#### Other

| Operation | Id | Who does it | Why it cannot be an API call | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Transfer the app to another App Store Connect account | `apple:app-transfer` | You or your agent | App transfers are initiated and accepted in the console. The public API exposes no transfer resource, and the operation moves an app — with its users, reviews and subscriptions — between two legal entities. | 2026-08-03 |

#### The app record

| Operation | Id | Who does it | Why it cannot be an API call | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Create the app record in App Store Connect | `apple:create-app-record` | You or your agent | The App Store Connect API manages apps that already exist; it has no endpoint that creates one. The app record, its bundle ID and its SKU are created in the console. | 2026-08-03 |

#### Account and enrollment

| Operation | Id | Who does it | Why it cannot be an API call | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Enrol in the Apple Developer Program | `apple:developer-enrollment` | You, personally | Enrolment is a paid legal agreement between Apple and a verified individual or organisation. There is no API for it, and Apple verifies identity out of band (D-U-N-S number for an organisation, government ID for an individual). It costs money, it binds the user legally, and it requires their Apple Account with two-factor authentication. No agent may sign a contract or handle someone's identity documents. | 2026-08-03 |

#### Review

| Operation | Id | Who does it | Why it cannot be an API call | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Release the approved version to the App Store | `apple:release-version` | You or your agent | Releasing a version Apple is holding for manual release goes through the appStoreVersionReleaseRequests endpoint, which the pinned `asc` does not expose. Agentship will not improvise a command against a live App Store account. | 2026-08-03 |
| Read and answer App Review messages | `apple:resolution-center` | You or your agent | Reviewer messages, attachments and rejection detail live in Resolution Center. The public API exposes only a coarse submission state, so the reason a version was rejected is not readable any other way. | 2026-08-03 |

### Google Play

#### Account and enrollment

| Operation | Id | Who does it | Why it cannot be an API call | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Complete the developer account, identity verification and payments profile | `google:account-and-payments` | You, personally | The one-time registration fee, identity verification and the payments profile are handled in Play Console by the account owner. Google exposes no API for any of them. It costs money, it requires government identity documents (and, for an organisation, a D-U-N-S number and a verified phone number), and it creates a payments profile tied to one named person. An agent must never handle identity documents or bank details. | 2026-08-03 |
| Run the closed test a new personal account needs before production | `google:closed-testing-requirement` | You, personally | Google requires a personal developer account created after 13 November 2023 to run a closed test with at least 12 testers who opted in, continuously for 14 days, and then to apply for production access. It is an account-level policy gate with no API. It is a waiting period and an application Google reviews, not an operation. Nobody can shorten it, and the testers have to be real people who actually opt in. | 2026-08-03 |

#### Privacy declarations

| Operation | Id | Who does it | Why it cannot be an API call | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Complete the App content declarations | `google:app-content` | You or your agent | Target audience, ads, news, government apps, financial features, health and the data safety review are answered in Play Console. Only the Data Safety form itself has an API (`applications.dataSafety`); the surrounding declarations do not. | 2026-08-03 |

#### Other

| Operation | Id | Who does it | Why it cannot be an API call | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Create a closed testing track and invite testers by e-mail | `google:closed-track-setup` | You or your agent | The Play Developer API assigns builds to tracks and manages tester *lists*, but it cannot create a custom closed track, and it addresses testers through Google Groups rather than individual e-mail addresses. A per-e-mail tester list is console work. | 2026-08-03 |

#### Content rating

| Operation | Id | Who does it | Why it cannot be an API call | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Complete the IARC content rating questionnaire | `google:content-rating` | You or your agent | Content ratings are issued by IARC, not by Google, through a questionnaire the developer answers under their own name. There is no API, and the answers are a declaration about the app's content. | 2026-08-03 |

#### The app record

| Operation | Id | Who does it | Why it cannot be an API call | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Create the app in Play Console | `google:create-app` | You or your agent | The Google Play Developer API operates on apps that already exist. Creating the app, and choosing its package name, is only possible in Play Console. | 2026-08-03 |
| Publish the first release from Play Console | `google:first-release` | You or your agent | Google requires a new app to reach its first release through the console. Until an app has been published once, API uploads to a track are rejected. | 2026-08-03 |

#### Review

| Operation | Id | Who does it | Why it cannot be an API call | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Publish the staged changes in Play Console | `google:managed-publishing` | You or your agent | With managed publishing on, Google holds every approved change until a human presses Publish in Play Console. There is no API for that button — that is the whole point of the setting. | 2026-08-03 |
| Read and answer a Play policy rejection | `google:policy-rejection` | You or your agent | Play exposes no review-status API at all. A rejection, the policy it cites and the appeal form exist only in Play Console and in the e-mail Google sends. | 2026-08-03 |

#### Credentials

| Operation | Id | Who does it | Why it cannot be an API call | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Enrol the app in Play App Signing | `google:play-app-signing` | You or your agent | Enrolment is a console operation with no API. It decides who holds the key that signs what users install, which is not something a tool may choose for a developer. | 2026-08-03 |

#### Pricing and availability

| Operation | Id | Who does it | Why it cannot be an API call | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Set the app price and the countries it is available in | `google:pricing-and-countries` | You or your agent | The Play Developer API prices in-app products, not the app itself. The app price, its free/paid status and its country availability are console-only. | 2026-08-03 |

## Things only you can do

- **Accept agreements and complete tax and banking details** (apple) — These are legal acceptances and financial identity details tied to one named person. An agent must never accept an agreement on someone's behalf, and must never see or type a bank account, a tax identifier or an identity document.
- **Create the App Store Connect API key** (apple) — Creating the key requires a signed-in App Store Connect session with two-factor authentication, and the download hands over a private key. Agentship stores that key through agentship_configure_auth and never sees the console session.
- **Enrol in the Apple Developer Program** (apple) — It costs money, it binds the user legally, and it requires their Apple Account with two-factor authentication. No agent may sign a contract or handle someone's identity documents.
- **Complete the developer account, identity verification and payments profile** (google) — It costs money, it requires government identity documents (and, for an organisation, a D-U-N-S number and a verified phone number), and it creates a payments profile tied to one named person. An agent must never handle identity documents or bank details.
- **Run the closed test a new personal account needs before production** (google) — It is a waiting period and an application Google reviews, not an operation. Nobody can shorten it, and the testers have to be real people who actually opt in.

## Two limits worth knowing before you start

- A new personal Google Play developer account must run a closed test with at least 12
  testers for 14 continuous days before it may publish to production. There is no way
  around it; plan for it.
- Apple issues the App Store Connect `.p8` key file exactly once. If it is lost, the key
  must be revoked and a new one generated.

## Platforms

Agentship runs on macOS and Linux, on x64 and arm64. Windows is not supported. Building an
`.ipa` requires macOS with Xcode; everything else — including the whole Google Play side
and every store operation for iOS — works anywhere, and a build produced elsewhere can be
published by pointing `release.artifacts` at the file.
